analysis.one_liner: Sends families a fully refundable monthly tax credit of up to $300 per child.
analysis.headline: The bill had 211 cosponsors — 211 of 216 House Democrats — but never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Ways and Means Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The American Family Act would replace the existing child tax credit with a new, fully refundable monthly credit: $250 per month for each child age 6 to 17 and $300 per month for each child under 6, sent throughout the year rather than once at tax time. Because the credit is fully refundable, families with little or no income tax bill would still get the full amount. It also adds a $500 credit for other dependents, adjusts the amounts for inflation, and phases down only for higher incomes. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, especially low- and middle-income families. Full refundability means the families with the least income — who currently get little or nothing from the child tax credit — would get the full monthly payments, and monthly delivery spreads the money across the year instead of one tax-season lump sum.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income families with children

how_it_helps.text: Creates a monthly credit of $250 per child age 6 to 17 and $300 per child under 6, paid monthly rather than once a year.
Makes the credit fully refundable, so families with little or no federal income tax liability receive the full amount — the current credit gives the least to the families with the least income.
Adds a $500 nonrefundable credit for other dependents, such as older teens in school or adult dependents.
Indexes the credit amounts and income thresholds to inflation, and includes protections against payments being garnished by most creditors.

analysis.who_pays: The bill contains no tax increase or spending cut to offset its cost, so the expense would be carried by federal borrowing — spread across taxpayers generally and future budgets — unless Congress separately passed legislation to pay for it. Households above the income thresholds ($150,000 for married couples, $112,500 for others before phase-downs begin) would receive reduced or no payments.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no revenue offset: it creates a large permanent benefit solely by adding to the deficit, leaving the question of who eventually pays for it to future legislation.

Monthly advance payments are based on prior-year income, so families whose income rises during the year — or who marry or change filing status — can receive too much and owe some of it back at tax time.
Payments phase down for higher-income households, and eligibility depends on annual renewal and documentation rules that could cause some eligible families to miss payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to families with children is large and well-targeted: full refundability concentrates the money on families with the least income, and monthly delivery makes it usable for rent, food, and childcare as those bills come due. The serious weakness is the financing — the bill provides a permanent entitlement with no dedicated revenue, so the roughly hundred-billion-dollar-a-year cost would be added to the deficit unless separately offset. An honest case for the bill has to argue that the anti-poverty benefit justifies the borrowing, or that Congress should pair it with revenue measures; the bill itself does not do the latter.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the American Family Act in the House on June 7, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax credits.
211 of the 216 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors — essentially the entire Democratic caucus — along with the sponsor; no Republicans cosponsored.
The committee took no further action of any kind: the full action history shows only the introduction and the referral to committee.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No industry or interest gained from the bill's death — the status quo simply held. Families with children forwent the monthly payments, and the immediate beneficiaries of inaction were those opposed to expanding deficit-financed spending, since the bill contained no revenue offset for its cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Deficit status quo; families lost the payments

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Family Act and organized the near-unanimous Democratic sponsorship.

for.name: 211 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — 211 of the 216 House Democrats then serving, with no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never held a hearing or markup and the bill never left committee.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Held the House majority and controlled the floor agenda in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, which it could not have reached without favorable committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely one-sided: 211 of 216 House Democrats cosponsored and no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chair, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill creates a permanent monthly child benefit with no tax increase or spending cut to pay for it, so the cost would be financed by borrowing. The same families the bill helps are also part of the taxpaying public that ultimately carries federal debt.

industries.industry: Higher-income households (above roughly $150,000-$400,000 depending on filing status)
industries.note: The credit phases down and phases out above income thresholds, so affluent households would receive little or nothing while the benefit is concentrated on lower- and middle-income families.
